theme: Sinai; the Ten Commandments, law after redemption
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 19:1-20:26. This is Mount Sinai, the giving of the Ten Commandments. Pay close attention to the order: first God describes what he has done, then he describes who they are, and only then does he give the commandments.
settingTheScene: Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel arrives at Mount Sinai. It is the turning point of the whole book. Everything before this point was rescue. Everything after is covenant, the formal relationship between God and Israel. The next several chapters are among the most important in the Old Testament, because they set out the terms of the Mosaic covenant. At the center is the Decalogue, the Ten Commandments. This is the day to remember that God redeems before he commands.
observation: God says through Moses, “You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles” wings and brought you to myself’ (19:4).
“Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine” (19:5).
“And you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (19:6).
The people answer together, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (19:8).
The people are consecrated, and boundaries are set around the mountain (19:10-13).
On the third day, there is thunder and lightning, a thick cloud, and a loud trumpet blast. “Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire” (19:16-18).
God speaks: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (20:2).

The commandments: no other gods; no carved images; do not take the LORD’s name in vain; remember the Sabbath; honor your father and mother; do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet (20:3-17).
The people tremble and say to Moses, “You speak to us, and we will hear; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die” (20:19).
Moses says, “Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin” (20:20).
interpretation:
Look at the order. In chapter 19, before a single commandment is given, God reminds Israel of what he has done: “You have seen…how I bore you on eagles” wings and brought you to myself.’ The same pattern is in 20:2. The commandments begin with a statement of redemption, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” This is the key to the entire law. It is not a ladder by which slaves climb to freedom. It is the way of life for people who have already been freed. This is the pattern of grace establishing law, and it is the theme of the unit.

God’s description of Israel in 19:5-6 is breathtaking. “My treasured possession.” “A kingdom of priests and a holy nation.” They are chosen out of all the peoples, set apart, and given a mission. They are to be priests, mediating between God and the nations. The New Testament will apply this same language to the church (1 Peter 2:9).

The people respond with eagerness: “All that the LORD has spoken we will do.” It is a sincere answer, and it is a disastrously overconfident one. They have not yet understood what they promised. Within forty days they will be dancing around a golden calf. It is one of the key tragedies of the Old Testament: the people said yes without understanding the cost.

The scene at the mountain is meant to communicate holiness. The boundaries, the fire, the smoke, the thunder, and the trumpet all say the same thing: God is not safe. The people are frightened, and rightly so. Their request that Moses speak for them is a request for a mediator. God approves it in Deuteronomy 18:17. A mediator will stand between them and the holy God. This points forward to Christ.

The Ten Commandments themselves are a summary of what it means to love God and love your neighbor. The first four concern God: his exclusive worship, his image, his name, and his day. The last six concern people: family, life, marriage, property, truth, and the heart’s desire. The tenth, “You shall not covet,” is the one that goes deepest, because it is about what the heart wants, and no human court can enforce it.

Moses’ last word at the end of the chapter is a paradox. “Do not fear…that the fear of him may be before you.” There is a fear that is terror, and a fear that is reverence. God does not want his people to cower. He wants them to stand in awe.
connection: Jesus summarized the law as love for God and love for neighbor (Matthew 22:37-40). Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts Mount Sinai, the mountain of fear, with Mount Zion, where we come to “Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant.” Peter calls the church “a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). Paul says that the law was “added because of transgressions” (Galatians 3:19), pointing to Christ.
application:
Say the Ten Commandments aloud, or read them slowly, and ask which one most clearly shows your need of grace. Do not rush through this step.

Notice that the first words are not “You shall” but “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out.” Receive that sentence as a statement about you if you are in Christ.

Think about how you tend to say “all that the LORD has spoken we will do” without counting the cost. Ask God for a humble and honest heart.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he redeems before he commands.
Tell him where you find his commands hard.
Thank Jesus for keeping the law you could not.
